# FDG9130

> DO prefer using `TimeSpan` to represent timeout time.

Framework Design Guidelines, 3rd edition, section 9.10 Timeouts.

## How it is checked

- Check: fdg (partial coverage)
- Diagnostics: FDG9130
- Automatic fix: not applied automatically (the fix can break callers)
- Severity: library warning, application warning, test none
- Status: draft

Message: Represent the timeout '{0}' of '{1}' with TimeSpan rather than '{2}'

FDG9130 reports an externally visible parameter (of a method, constructor, indexer or delegate) or property whose type is an integer type (sbyte, byte, short, ushort, int, uint, long or ulong) and whose name ends with the word Timeout (timeout, ReadTimeout), unless a word of the name is a unit of time (Milliseconds, Millisecond, Ms, Msec, Microseconds, Microsecond, Seconds, Second, Secs, Sec, Minutes, Minute, Mins, Hours, Hour, Days, Day, Ticks or Tick, as in millisecondsTimeout or TimeoutMs), the first case in which the body accepts integer timeouts. The second condition of the body, a commonly used value small enough to need no calculator, is not checked, so a timeout whose name gives its unit is never reported. Timeouts whose name does not end with Timeout, fields, and the parameters and properties of overrides and interface implementations, whose names and types come from another member, are not reported, so coverage is partial. Changing the type changes the public signature, so the fix is breaking; there is no code fix.

## From the book

Historically, timeouts have been represented by integers. Integer timeouts can be hard to use for the following reasons:

- It is not obvious what the unit of the timeout is.
- It is difficult to translate units of time into the commonly used millisecond. (How many milliseconds are in 15 minutes?)

Often, a better approach is to use `TimeSpan` as the timeout type. `TimeSpan` solves the preceding problems.

```csharp
class Server {
  void PerformOperation(TimeSpan timeout){
  ...
  }
}

var server = new Server();
server.PerformOperation(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(15));
```

Integer timeouts are acceptable if:

- The parameter or property name can describe the unit of time used by the operation—for example, if a parameter can be called `milliseconds` without making an otherwise self-describing API cryptic.
- The most commonly used value is small enough that users won’t have to use calculators to determine the value—for example, if the unit is milliseconds and the commonly used timeout is less than 1 second.
